events.subject: Plan the week, still post today
events.preview_text: Line posts up ahead and slide in today's news without starting over.
events.body:
Buffer lets you line up a couple of weeks of posts and still post the moment something happens in the shop.

Here's how it works. You set your posting times and fill a queue with your Facebook and Instagram posts. When something timely comes up, you add it and drag the rest back into order.

So you're never stuck with what you scheduled. On a busy day the post you meant to write is the first thing to slip — here you just slide today's update in and let the rest keep rolling.

The Free plan holds **10 scheduled posts per channel** at a time. Once a post publishes, that slot opens back up. Worth a look to see whether that covers the weekly queue you have in mind.
events.call_to_action: See what the Free plan includes
events.postscript: The Free plan is free forever, so you can look before you build anything.

events.subject: The week your page went quiet
events.preview_text: Line up two weeks of posts, still post what happens in the shop today.
events.body:
You keep the shop's social going yourself — a post here, a post there, whenever a quiet minute shows up.

That works until the week gets busy. Posting one at a time is the first thing to drop when the counter's full, and the page goes quiet for a stretch.

Buffer is scheduling software that lets you line up a couple of weeks of posts for your Facebook and Instagram pages, then drop in whatever happens in the shop today.

You click the timely post into the queue, drag the rest back into order, and your plan reshuffles around it — nothing is locked to the slot you first gave it.

Foster Coffee, a two-location Michigan coffee shop, found two weeks to be their sweet spot — far enough ahead to stay ahead, close enough to add something last-minute.

Before you build a week's queue, it's worth checking the limits. The Free plan holds **10 scheduled posts per channel** at once, and a slot opens back up each time a post publishes.
events.postscript: The page lays out what each plan includes — a look at the limits, not a walkthrough of building the queue.

edits.line: Buffer is scheduling software that lets you line up a couple of weeks of posts for your Facebook and Instagram pages, then drop in whatever happens in the shop today.

events.summary: Buffer is social scheduling software — you queue up a week of Facebook and Instagram posts ahead of time and can reorder them when something comes up, so your page doesn't go quiet when the shop gets busy.
issues: 'Planning a week of posts ahead can feel like a big-brand, marketing-team thing.' — opens with an abstraction; lead instead with the busy-shop moment that's concrete to me.
'Nothing is locked to the slot you first gave it — the plan reshuffles around today.' — reads like a riddle on a busy morning; say plainly 'drag a post and the rest shift down.'
'Before you build your first week, see whether that allowance matches how often you post.' — makes me do mental math before I've even clicked; just tell me what fits a once-a-day shop.
events.biggest_doubt: Whether lining up a week of posts is worth the setup effort when my posts barely reach anyone anyway — plus it's a busy Tuesday and learning a new tool isn't a three-minute job.
events.stopped_at: Foster Coffee, a two-location Michigan coffee shop, runs its social on Buffer

readers.what_it_sells: Buffer is social scheduling software with a free plan that lets me queue up a week of Facebook and Instagram posts ahead of time and reshuffle them when something comes up in the shop.
readers.biggest_doubt: Effort versus payoff: setting up a scheduler and building a week of posts is still my time, and I'm not sure consistent posting changes how few people actually see them. The email sells smoother scheduling but says nothing about reach.

'Before you build your first week, see whether that allowance matches how often you post.' — adds a homework step before the click; replace with how quickly I can connect a page and get one week queued.
'Foster Coffee, a two-location Michigan coffee shop, runs its social on Buffer' — name what it changed for them (how much time, or that the page stopped going quiet), otherwise it's just a logo.
